All right. Good afternoon and happy Friday, everyone. As you know, the Secretary-General is in New Delhi for the BRICS Summit, and he met there today with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi. The Secretary-General reaffirmed the principle of freedom of navigation. The two leaders also had an exchange of views on the growing danger of lethal autonomous weapons. The Secretary-General will deliver remarks at the summit on Sunday, and we will share those with you when we can. I have the following statement on the passing of William Henry Draper. The Secretary-General was saddened to learn of the passing of former UN Development Programme Administrator William Henry Draper. Mr. Draper served as UNDP administrator from 1986 to 1993. He was a true champion of the world's poorest people and supported a significant expansion of UNDP's development work. Under his leadership, UNDP launched the first Human Development Report in 1990, which shifted the focus of development approach from a narrow one based on economic growth to a wider look at the range of factors affecting human well-being. The Secretary-General offers his condolences to Mr. Draper's family and friends, and to all those who worked with him to improve the living conditions of people around the world. Our Under-Secretary-General for Peace Operations, Jean-Pierre Lacroix, was in Lianyungang, China, until today, where he participated in the 2026 Conference of the Global Public Security Cooperation Forum. Addressing the forum, Mr. LeCoeur reaffirmed his conviction that no country can face today's complex security challenges alone. He said international cooperation is the way forward and thanked China for convening this important event. While there, Mr. LeCoeur also met with China's State Councilor and Minister of Public Security, Wang Xiaohong. He expressed appreciation for China's continued political and financial support to peace operations. which allows us to deliver on mandates and pilot innovation. Natalia Germann, Executive Director of the Counter-Terrorism Executive Directorate, and Ehab Omash, Representative of the UN Office on Counter-Terrorism, will brief the Council. Turning to Yemen, we are gravely concerned by the seizure of a key humanitarian common premises and its assets in Mocha by the Houthi de facto authorities. The compound houses staff of UN agencies working to provide humanitarian assistance to vulnerable communities in the area. All UN personnel working at the common premises had left the compound before the seizure and are safe and accounted for. We reiterate that humanitarian personnel, premises, and assets must be respected and protected at all times. Safe and unimpeded humanitarian access must also be ensured so that lifesaving assistance can continue to reach people in need, particularly at this critical time. We remain committed to supporting Yemeni vulnerable communities. Meanwhile, our humanitarian colleagues on the ground tell us that civilians continue to flee the fighting. 18,000 households have been displaced since the start of the month. People are reportedly moving towards the governorates of Taiz, Aden, Lahj, and Abyan. We and our humanitarian partners are working to respond, but access and funding constraints continue to pose severe challenges. For example, our partners working to mobilize rapid response efforts have 15,000 emergency kits ready to go, but cuts to roads mean the majority are stuck in Aden. The Mokha seaport sustained significant damage during the recent fighting, and operations there are suspended. Once again, we call on all parties to protect civilians, respect international humanitarian law, and facilitate safe and unimpeded humanitarian access so that urgently needed assistance can reach communities in need. And just to flag that yesterday afternoon, Hans Grunberg, the special envoy for Yemen, briefed the Security Council on the situation in Yemen and the developments in Mocha. He called on Ansar Allah to cease its attacks inside Yemen and across the border into the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, and to cease attacks and threats against commercial vessels. He added that he will continue to engage the government of Yemen and the Houthis to identify feasible ways forward, adding that he will work in close partnership with regional actors whose engagement is indispensable to help contain the situation. Turning to the occupied Palestinian territory, the Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs tells us that yesterday the UN and our partners brought into Gaza more than 350,000 liters of fuel and collected hundreds of pallets of supplies from the Kerem Shalom-Karem Abu Salem crossing. This assistance included antibiotics and other medical supplies, breast pumps, medical equipment, winter clothes, and school bags. The teams also supported the medical evacuation of dozens of patients and their companions. In addition, humanitarian partners offered psychological first aid, emergency assistance, and referral services to Palestinians who had previously been unable to return to Gaza. Meanwhile, our partners leading on displacement site management have been prepared for the coming winter. Last week, they reinforced shelters, improved drainage, maintained pathways, and carried out other small-scale preparations at displacement sites, despite limited capacity and lack of machinery. Our partners are also collecting and distributing wooden pallets and empty flour sacks that can be filled with sand to reduce the potential impact of heavy rainfall, flooding, and strong winds. However, the International Organization for Migration has warned that shortages of some 8.6 million items required for the winter, including tarpaulins, mattresses, sandbags, plywood, and repair toolkits, mean that more than 1.5 million people could go without winter assistance at current funding levels. Across the occupied Palestinian territory, humanitarian efforts this year are less than 40% funded. Turning to the West Bank, more than 830,000 boys and girls returned to school this week. Among them are more than 4,000 students who have been displaced from refugee camps in the northern West Bank and not allowed to return. Schooling is also affected by the closure of six UN Relief and Works Agency schools in East Jerusalem by the Israeli authorities. Turning to Lebanon, where hostilities continue to cause further destruction and damage to civilian infrastructure in the south. In the municipality of Mansouri in South Governorate, a public school was largely destroyed overnight, following several days of intense demolition activity in the area, according to local authorities. And last night, large explosions were reported in south of Nabatiya city, following the reported destruction of underground tunnels. The blasts were felt across parts of southern Lebanon and caused civilian harm and concern among communities. Renewed fighting is also affecting people trying to return home. In Al-Nabatiyah District, our partners recorded nearly 29,000 people over the past week, a drop of 13%. The decline may indicate that renewed insecurity is discouraging some families from returning, while others who had already returned may now be fleeing again. Humanitarian access remains difficult, but there's been one positive development. Yesterday, for the first time since the 29th of July, a humanitarian convoy received clearance through the humanitarian notification system to reach border villages that have faced prolonged access constraints. OSCE reiterates the need to protect civilians and civilian infrastructure, and says continued hostilities are preventing people from returning safely and sustainably. He also met the Speaker of the People's Assembly to discuss its work and UN support. Mr. Cordone traveled to Aleppo, Tartus, Latakia, and Idlib, where he met with the governors, various interlocutors, and civil society organizations. Discussions focused on issues related to recovery, reconstruction, returns, transitional justice, and social cohesion. From Ukraine, our colleagues at the Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs tell us that civilians, including children, continue to be killed and injured in attacks and frontline hostilities. Homes, businesses, and other civilian infrastructure also sustained damage across the country. The Dnipro region was hardest hit, with most casualties reported in Pavlohrad, where a shopping mall in the city center was struck during the busy evening yesterday. The humanitarian coordinator for Ukraine, Matthias Schmale, stressed that people should be able to go about their daily lives safely and expressed his deepest condolences to the families who lost their loved ones. Elsewhere, attacks caused further casualties across the regions of Sumy, Donetsk, Kharkiv, Kherson, and Poltava. We, along with our humanitarian partners, are providing emergency shelter materials, psychosocial support, and hot meals for people impacted, as well as first responders. Our partners are also registering families, including those with children, for humanitarian cash assistance as the response continues. Turning to Sierra Leone, the Secretary-General has approved the Government's request to renew the country's eligibility for support from the Peacebuilding Fund for a further five years, through the end of 2030. The renewal will allow Sierra Leone to continue receiving targeted UN peacebuilding assistance and advance national efforts to prevent conflict, strengthen social cohesion, expand the role of women and young people in public life, deepen cross-border cooperation on peace, and address security risks linked to climate change and environmental pressures. In addition, the Peacebuilding Fund will provide $3 million to support the development and implementation of Sierra Leone's first national prevention strategy in partnership with the UN Development Programme, UNICEF and UN Women.
